analysis.title: Scarred For Life: Goldman Finds Workers Displaced By AI Stay Jobless Longer, Then Land In Jobs AI Will Take Next
key_insights: Goldman economist Pierfrancesco Mei finds that across nonmanufacturing industries, higher AI adoption is now associated with weaker employment growth and higher unemployment. The effect now includes finance, insurance, real estate and professional services, not only web hosting and computing.

Workers displaced from AI-exposed jobs take about a month longer to find new work and are roughly 10pp more likely to still be unemployed a year later. Goldman says the size matches earlier waves of technological change. The data show little effect through 2024 and a clear break in 2025.

The study uses the Census Bureau's Displaced Worker Supplement (over 15,000 displaced workers, 2016-2025). Goldman builds a composite AI-displacement score from occupation exposure, industry adoption and whether the position was eliminated, then compares the top 30% against all other displaced workers.

Earlier tech waves left lasting damage. A decade after displacement, older, non-college, rural and long-tenured workers were roughly 8-10 points behind other laid-off workers in cumulative real wages, about twice the gap of younger, college-educated, urban and short-tenured peers.

Younger workers are adapting better. In 2025, AI-displaced workers under 35 took about three weeks longer than other displaced workers to return to full-time work, against about five weeks for those 35 and older. College students are shifting toward majors tied to lower-AI-exposure occupations.

AI-displaced workers, especially older ones, increasingly move into roles with the same or higher AI exposure. The probability was in the mid-50s from 2018 through 2023, rose to about 65% in 2024 and to nearly 75% in 2025. Goldman attributes this to workers seeking jobs that use their existing skills.

BLS data show 7.4 million workers displaced in 2023-2025, up from 6.3 million in the prior survey. Among long-tenured displaced workers who found full-time jobs, about 49% earned as much or more than before, down from about 62%. Reemployment rates fall with age: 72.9% for ages 25-54, 57.3% for 55-64 and 38.6% for 65 and older.

Goldman's Joseph Briggs says concern about imminent AI displacement has cooled. Challenger AI-attributed layoffs peaked near 40K in May and fell below 5K in August and September. The unemployment rate was 4.2% in September.

Briggs finds each 1% boost to labor productivity from technology lifts the unemployment rate by 0.3-0.4pp at the peak, mostly through job losses rather than weaker hiring. Applied to Goldman's forecast of a 15% AI productivity gain, up to 9% of workers could be displaced, with slower hiring weighing on employment by a further 3%. That is roughly 15 million US workers, up from 6-7% earlier in the year.

Automation is cyclical. Routine-job headwinds have concentrated in recessions (early 1980s, 2001, 2008, 2020), and in tech-disrupted occupations each 1pp rise in unemployment added about 4% more job losses on a roughly 25% baseline. Briggs concludes a cyclical slowdown would likely accelerate AI-related automation and job losses.

Briggs suggests central banks stay attentive to downside growth and labor risks once the near-term inflation constraint lifts, so a quick pivot to easing could limit automation-related job losses. ZeroHedge notes Goldman still expects the Fed to hike again in December.

BofA's US economists expect AI's labor market impact to stay limited through '26, with broader reallocation more likely in '27, and forecast October payrolls of +75K, above consensus. Apollo's Slok found earlier that AI was hitting pay (6.7% slower growth in the most exposed jobs) rather than payrolls.

Only 23% of US establishments have built AI into some regular workflows, yet that adoption level has already produced statistically significant job losses outside tech. The report says effects should grow if adoption doubles or triples.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Headline unemployment has not yet reflected AI displacement. Goldman's Briggs argues the layoffs are likely to wait for a recession.
BofA expects limited AI labor impact through '26. The report treats the print as the next test of that view.

macro_indicators.indicator: Challenger job cuts attributed to AI
macro_indicators.reading: Peaked near 40K in May, below 5K in both August and September
macro_indicators.interpretation: AI-attributed layoffs have cooled since spring, though ZeroHedge notes October cuts at Barclays, Amex and FICO came after the chart was drawn.

macro_indicators.reading: Goldman expects another hike in December
macro_indicators.interpretation: A hiking Fed conflicts with Briggs' suggestion of a quick pivot to easing to limit automation-related job losses.
Drives the estimate that up to 9% of workers could be displaced during the AI transition.

risk_factors: A recession could trigger a catch-up wave of AI-related layoffs on top of normal cyclical layoffs.
The AI capex boom is now a main support for growth and Goldman's Hatzius warns the impulse is peaking, which could itself help trigger a downturn.
Higher AI adoption would enlarge displacement effects. AI capex is largely debt-financed, so adoption could stall.
A Fed that is still hiking limits room for the quick pivot to easing Briggs says would soften automation-related job losses.
Displaced workers re-entering equally AI-exposed roles face repeat displacement.
charts_described: Probability that a worker displaced from an AI-risk job lands in a role with the same or higher AI exposure hovered in the mid-50s from 2018 through 2023, then rose to about 65% in 2024 and nearly 75% in 2025.
Chart of workers most likely displaced by AI shows little difference through 2024 and a clear break in 2025 in time to find a job and unemployment one year later.

Chart of cumulative real wage gap a decade after displacement (1979-2022) shows older, non-college, rural and long-tenured workers roughly 8-10 points behind other laid-off workers, about twice the gap of younger, college-educated, urban and short-tenured peers.
Chart of the share of Americans in routine jobs shows it held flat through each expansion and dropped in steps in the early 1980s, 2001, 2008 and 2020 without recovering.

tension_points.bull_case: BofA's US economists expect AI's labor market impact to stay limited through '26, with broader reallocation in '27. Challenger AI-attributed layoffs fell below 5K in August and September, and Apollo's Slok found AI hit paychecks rather than payrolls.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman finds higher industry AI adoption is now tied to weaker employment growth and higher unemployment, and displaced workers face longer joblessness. Briggs estimates up to 9% of workers could be displaced, with layoffs likely waiting for a recession.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A cyclical slowdown or recession, which Briggs says would likely accelerate AI-related automation and job losses.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman says younger workers are handling the transition better (about three weeks longer to return to full-time work versus about five for those 35 and older) and students are moving to lower-AI-exposure majors.
tension_points.bear_case: Displaced workers increasingly land in equally or more AI-exposed roles (nearly 75% in 2025), and young entrants in exposed occupations are not being hired, with employment about 19% below counterfactual.

theme_stances.key_argument: Higher industry AI adoption is now linked to weaker employment growth and higher unemployment, and displaced workers face longer and more difficult transitions.
theme_stances.evidence: higher AI adoption is now associated with weaker employment growth and higher unemployment

theme_stances.key_argument: Routine-job automation headwinds concentrate in recessions, so a slowdown would likely bring pent-up AI layoffs all at once.
theme_stances.evidence: a cyclical slowdown would likely accelerate AI-related automation and job losses
